governing_thought: DCCE must formally accept four continuing institutional roles before the platform enters its next development phase, because the evidence in this chapter shows the content and data gaps documented here -- most urgently the ones blocking DCCE's mandatory UNFCCC A-BTR report -- are gaps in ongoing institutional practice, not gaps a one-off system build can close; only DCCE itself, holding product ownership, data governance, inter-agency data integration, and national adaptation reporting authority continuously, can keep them closed.

narrative_scqa.situation: DCCE is Thailand's national focal point for climate change adaptation and, on that basis, carries a direct, recurring UNFCCC transparency-reporting obligation (the Adaptation Biennial Transparency Report, A-BTR). The consultant has already defined 9 priority climate information services for the platform, 8 of which were validated directly against real user-agency demand through WP6 interviews and workshops.
narrative_scqa.complication: When the consultant checked DCCE's actual content and data holdings against what the approved website sitemap and the A-BTR reporting obligation require, most of the needed content turned out not to exist: only 16 of 75 required topics are publication-ready, and the specific data-management functions A-BTR reporting depends on -- cross-cycle data lineage, event-level loss-and-damage records, climate budget tagging, and private climate-finance tracking -- are missing altogether. This shortfall sits alongside, not in place of, the demand-side gap already surfaced through WP6, and it was not visible until this content-by-content check was done.
narrative_scqa.question: Given that this shortfall threatens DCCE's ability to meet a binding, recurring international reporting obligation, what must DCCE decide now, before committing to the platform's next development phase?
narrative_scqa.answer: DCCE must formally accept four continuing institutional roles -- product owner of the platform, data governance lead, inter-agency data integration hub, and national adaptation reporting authority -- because closing the content and data gaps this chapter documents requires DCCE to exercise these functions on an ongoing basis, not to procure another system build.

argument_units.claim: DCCE's institutional role as Thailand's national focal point for climate change adaptation, and the direct UNFCCC reporting obligation this creates under the Enhanced Transparency Framework, is the reason this chapter treats the Adaptation Biennial Transparency Report (A-BTR) as its central forcing case rather than as one item among nine equally-weighted services.
argument_units.grounds: Thailand's own draft Adaptation chapter for the 5th National Communication / 2nd Biennial Transparency Report (5NC/2BTR, second interim report) states directly that DCCE serves as the National Focal Point for climate change adaptation, and describes DCCE coordinating, monitoring, and periodically reporting NAP progress under the Enhanced Transparency Framework -- the same source the A-BTR institutional-baseline requirement extraction is built on.
argument_units.warrant: A reporting duty owed directly to an international body on a fixed biennial cycle cannot be deferred or delegated the way an internally-prioritized service can; because DCCE itself, not an external requester, bears this obligation, any gap that blocks A-BTR compilation is a compliance risk specific to DCCE. That is why this chapter must elevate A-BTR above the chapter's other findings rather than fold it into the general service narrative.
argument_units.application_to_design: The section's opening must state the A-BTR obligation as the chapter's organizing rationale before any other content is introduced, and the platform blueprint must treat A-BTR's data requirements as a fixed, non-negotiable content set rather than a discretionary one to be prioritized against demand signals.

argument_units.claim: Of the nine climate information services this platform must deliver, eight were distilled from real user-agency demand through direct interviews and workshops (WP6 Service Intelligence), while the ninth -- A-BTR reporting -- originates entirely differently: from DCCE's own obligation to UNFCCC, not from any external request, so DCCE must build it and supply most of its own inputs regardless of how it would rank against demand-side prioritization signals.
argument_units.grounds: The WP6 report (บทสรุปความต้องการใช้งานบริการข้อมูลสารสนเทศด้านภูมิอากาศ_v6) documents the 8 services being distilled from direct engagement with external user agencies; the A-BTR use-case pipeline document and the 5NC/2BTR institutional baseline establish that the ninth service originates in DCCE's own reporting duty to UNFCCC rather than in any agency request captured in WP6.
argument_units.warrant: Because the two groups of services have structurally different origins -- one validated by demonstrated external demand, one owed regardless of demand -- a demand-based prioritization logic appropriate for the first 8 services would wrongly deprioritize the 9th if applied uniformly to all nine. This is why A-BTR needs its own explanatory paragraph rather than being folded into the demand-derived service narrative.
argument_units.application_to_design: The platform blueprint and roadmap must not gate A-BTR-related content and data work behind the same demand-validation process used for the other 8 services; it must instead be scheduled and resourced against the UNFCCC reporting cycle.

argument_units.claim: Against the 75 content topics the approved website sitemap requires, only 16 topics (21%) are publication-ready, 26 (35%) are partially populated, and 33 (44%) are entirely unsupported by DCCE's existing holdings -- close to 8 in 10 topics still need fresh research or drafting, which contradicts the prior assumption that DCCE already holds the needed content and only needs to publish it.
argument_units.grounds: The WP4 Content-Source Gap Analysis v2 compared each of the 75 sitemap-mandated topics, one by one, against what actually exists in DCCE's document repositories and databases, and classified each topic as ready, partial, or gap, producing the 16/26/33 split.
argument_units.warrant: Because this 75-topic content structure is what the 9 demand-validated services -- including A-BTR -- depend on to function on the platform, a supply-side shortfall of this size means the platform cannot yet deliver on demand already established through WP6. The content gap is therefore not an isolated web-publishing detail; it is the concrete measure of how far current supply falls short of validated demand.
argument_units.application_to_design: Content development planning must treat the 33 fully-missing and 26 partially-populated topics as a dedicated research-and-drafting work stream, sized and sequenced ahead of system-build activity, rather than as incidental content migration.

argument_units.claim: The same topic-by-topic comparison that produced the 75-topic readiness split shows that 47 of those 75 topics are directly tied to A-BTR reporting content, meaning the content shortfall is not a general website-completeness problem but a direct threat to a binding UNFCCC obligation.
argument_units.grounds: WP4 Content-Source Gap Analysis v2 cross-references the 75-topic sitemap set against A-BTR-linked content requirements and identifies the 47-topic subset that A-BTR reporting depends on.
argument_units.warrant: Because close to two-thirds of the overall content gap is content A-BTR itself needs, closing the general website content gap and reducing DCCE's A-BTR compliance risk are substantially the same task. That overlap is why this finding belongs in the chapter's institutional argument, not only in a website-completeness discussion.
argument_units.application_to_design: The 47 A-BTR-linked topics must be flagged and sequenced ahead of the remaining 28 general-content topics in the content-development backlog handed to the next project phase.

argument_units.claim: Even where DCCE already holds climate projection and risk data, it still cannot compile an auditable A-BTR, because four distinct data-management functions the report depends on are absent -- these are gaps in institutional data practice, not gaps in written content: (1) no system records the provenance of reported figures across the two-year reporting cycle, so a figure cannot be traced back to its originating source when the next report is due; (2) no event-level loss-and-damage database exists, so loss-and-damage figures cannot be reported at the granularity UNFCCC review expects; (3) no climate budget-tagging system classifies public expenditure by climate purpose, so adaptation-finance figures cannot be substantiated; (4) no mechanism tracks private-sector climate finance or technology transfer, leaving that reporting category unsupported.
argument_units.grounds: The WP7 Gap Analysis Report (2026-08-16) extends the demand-supply gap analysis to 11 supply-side dimensions and traces their impact on the 9 services, identifying these four functions -- cross-cycle data lineage, event-level loss-and-damage data, climate budget tagging, and private climate-finance/technology tracking -- as the specific dimensions blocking A-BTR compilation.
argument_units.warrant: Because A-BTR must be auditable end to end -- every reported figure traceable to its source -- for UNFCCC review, the absence of any one of these four functions breaks the reporting chain regardless of how complete the surrounding narrative content becomes. That is why finishing the website's written content, however thorough, cannot by itself close DCCE's A-BTR compliance risk; the four functions are data-management infrastructure, not content.
argument_units.application_to_design: The bottleneck-chain figure required for this section must render each of the four functions as a distinct blocking node between the content gap and A-BTR completion, and the platform's data-governance workstream, not its content workstream, must own closing each one.

argument_units.claim: Because the gaps documented above are gaps in continuous institutional practice rather than in a one-off deliverable, DCCE must formally accept four institutional roles -- already endorsed in principle by DCCE leadership in the approved strategic-alignment framework -- before the platform enters its next development phase: (1) product owner of the national data platform, holding product vision and setting requirements for all 9 information services on an ongoing basis; (2) data governance lead, appointing data stewards in every division and certifying official data status through DCCE's own data governance committee; (3) inter-agency data integration hub, securing data-exchange agreements with the external agencies that hold most of the country's relevant data; (4) national adaptation reporting authority, using the platform as the single reference base to meet A-BTR and NAP reporting obligations to UNFCCC.
argument_units.grounds: The strategic-alignment deck DCCE leadership already approved (2026-06-11) sets out these four institutional roles and the underlying three-step delivery process; the content, demand, and bottleneck findings in this chapter (arg-01 through arg-05) supply the evidentiary case for why each role is needed now rather than deferred to a later phase.
argument_units.warrant: A system build, however complete, only produces a data platform; it does not itself keep data lineage current, certify new datasets, renegotiate external data-sharing terms, or decide what the next A-BTR cycle needs. Those are continuing decisions only DCCE, exercising these four roles on an ongoing basis, can make. Without DCCE holding them, the four bottlenecks diagnosed above will recur in every future reporting cycle regardless of what the next contractor builds.
argument_units.application_to_design: The report's concluding recommendation set must present these four roles as governance preconditions for the next procurement phase, not as post-launch operational detail, and the roadmap must schedule role assignment (naming data stewards, drafting data-exchange agreements) ahead of or alongside system-build activity.
